title: Slow-Moving Nor'easter Floods the Northeast, Cutting Power to 100,000
summary:
A powerful, slow-moving storm crawled along the northeast U.S. coast on Saturday, knocking out electricity to about 100,000 customers and flooding coastal towns. Tens of millions of people from the mid-Atlantic to New England were in the path of the nor'easter — a storm that forms along the East Coast — and forecasters warned there was no quick end in sight.

"There will be a lot of high winds, a lot of high tides and heavy rain possibility over the next few days," said Bob Oravec, lead forecaster with the National Weather Service in College Park, Maryland.

On the Jersey Shore, Kenny Formica, owner of Surf City Marina, watched through surveillance cameras as water rose inside his building. He said that's rare — the last time was Hurricane Sandy, which caused more than $4 million in damage to his business. Workers had tied down dock lines and parked trucks and forklifts on the highest ground. By Saturday morning, even those were nearly surrounded. "This is like an 8,000-pound boat and a $150,000 boat — just gone," he said.

In Edgewater, New Jersey, water spilled into a parking lot packed with cars. Video showed one car nearly submerged, with only its sunroof above the water.

The storm scrambled travel and sports. Hundreds of flights were cancelled at Boston Logan International Airport, and most flights to Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket were grounded. The Red Sox and Chicago Cubs played a double-header Friday, then moved their Sunday finale to Florida. Singer Ed Sheeran cancelled concerts at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts.

In North Carolina, a highway closure on Hatteras Island stranded most of the roughly 45 guests invited to Jayden Sink and Kimberly Laprad's wedding.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said coastal flooding is the biggest threat, with waves up to six metres. "The rain is underway, and while it's only half an inch or so thus far, mark my words: Much more is coming," she said.
why_it_matters: Extreme weather like this shows how fragile everyday systems — power, flights, roads and shops — can be, and it forces coastal communities to decide whether to keep rebuilding in flood zones or change how they live with the sea.

background_read: Nor'easters are not rare events: they form when cold air from the north collides with warmer ocean air along the U.S. East Coast, usually in late fall, winter or early spring, and they are known for heavy rain or snow, fierce winds and coastal flooding.

Hurricane Sandy (a huge 2012 storm that struck the U.S. East Coast) pushed a wall of seawater into New York and New Jersey and remains the benchmark coastal business owners use for 'the worst I have seen.'

The National Weather Service (the U.S. government agency that forecasts weather and issues official warnings) tracks these storms and can flag the dangers — wind, tides, rain — days in advance, which is why workers at the Jersey Shore had time to tie down dock lines and move equipment to high ground.
The Northeast is also densely populated and heavily dependent on air travel, so a storm that parks over the region can cancel hundreds of flights and force sports teams to move games far away.
Scientists say rising sea levels linked to climate change mean the same storm now floods more land than it would have a few decades ago, a pattern that keeps raising the damage done to coastal towns.

perspectives.description: Forecasters warned days ahead, and workers at the marina moved trucks and forklifts to high ground, showing that good warnings and planning can limit losses.

perspectives.perspective: Repeat victims are being left behind
perspectives.description: Small coastal businesses like Formica's marina have now been flooded twice in just over a decade, and each rebuild is harder to afford as insurance and repair costs climb.

perspectives.perspective: A normal storm, a changed coastline
perspectives.description: Nor'easters have always hit the East Coast, but more homes, roads and businesses now sit in flood-prone areas, and higher sea levels mean each storm reaches further inland than it once did.
Longer term, cities may need sea walls, restored wetlands and stricter building rules, while officials weigh whether some neighbourhoods can be protected at all.
